# Voice profile — doctorow-blog

> **Confidence: full** — 10 usable samples, 17,549 corpus words. voice.md is empty; all observations are derived from corpus.

## 1. Cadence

The ruling rhythm is: long setup, short verdict. A paragraph accumulates evidence or irony across two or three sentences; then a clause of five words or fewer delivers judgment and stops. After an extended explanation of how treating a worker without moral consideration functions: *"There's only one kind of person you get to treat like this: a slave"* (`2026-07-10-posthuman-as-in-no-humans.txt`). After three sentences of bureaucratic irony: *"DROP didn't get the memo"* (`2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt`). After a paragraph mapping Trump's negotiating pattern: *"For Trump, 'the art of the deal' can be summed up in one word: renege"* (`2026-07-22-table-flipper.txt`). 10/10 samples, several times per piece.

To use it: when you have been building for two or more sentences, write the next sentence in one clause, active voice, no qualifier. The shortness is the signal that this is the point.

Sentences otherwise range widely — expository passages can stretch across stacked subordinate clauses while verdict sentences sit under ten words. Length tracks purpose: complexity of setup earns long sentences; judgment earns short ones.

## 2. How a piece opens

Three shapes appear, none dominant:

**"Here's a X:"** (2/10 samples) — announces something found and names it. *"Here's an irony: the 'gig economy' is a statistical black hole"* (`2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`); *"Here's a sentence that stopped me in my tracks last week"* (`2026-07-22-table-flipper.txt`). The phrase is a hook; everything that follows is setup.

**Blunt declarative** (2/10 samples) — verdict before argument. *"Data brokers are a cancer"* (`2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt`); *"As a technology, AI isn't exceptional"* (`2026-07-24-supplemental-income.txt`). The rest of the piece substantiates rather than discovers.

**Names a concept and positions it for examination** (6/10 samples) — introduces a term or framework, then begins dismantling or extending it. *"The 'designated survivor' is one of the weirder aspects of America's (very, very weird) political system"* (`2026-07-14-designated-survivor.txt`); *"The theory of markets goes like this:"* (`2026-07-16-lucky-orifices.txt`); *"One of 2026's better tech-related coinages is 'dickover'"* (`2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`). The concept is named fairly; the piece is what happens after.

None of the ten openings begin with a qualification or concession.

## 3. How a piece closes

8/10 samples close by returning to a term from earlier in the piece — usually the opponent's own word — and repurposing it or delivering a compressed verdict inside it. In `2026-07-11-your-risk.txt`, the piece ends by taking the company's word "flexibility" and flipping it: *"they value their flexibility, which arises out of the constraints (technical, legal) they impose on us."* In `2026-07-16-lucky-orifices.txt`, the closing takes the accusation "billionaire derangement syndrome" and redirects it: *"the only 'billionaire derangement syndrome' that matters is the syndrome that affects billionaires."* In `2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`: *"What they call 'theft' is just self-defense."*

If you are writing a close: find the word the opponent owns in this piece, name it, and deliver a sentence that turns it. Keep that sentence short.

## 4. Who is being addressed, and how

Second person is the dominant grammatical mode. Counting case-insensitive whole-word *you, your, yours, you're, you've, you'd, you'll* ([measurement:second-person-family]): 385 tokens, 21.94 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. The "you" addresses the reader as someone already caught in the systems the piece describes — the gig economy extracts from *you*, the surveillance apparatus spies on *you*.

Alongside "you" sits an inclusive first-person plural. Counting *we, us, our, ours* and contracted forms, excluding uppercase US ([measurement:first-person-plural-family]): 127 tokens, 7.24 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. *"We got rid of pop-ups by installing pop-up blockers"* (`2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`). "You" addresses the reader as the target of a system; "we" places writer and reader as co-actors against it. Both rates should be hit.

First-person singular — counting *I, me, my, mine, myself* ([measurement:first-person-singular-family]): 113 tokens, 6.44 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. The writer appears as a person with opinions, not an impersonal analyst.

**Contraction is near-total.** Counting *n't, 're, 've, 'll, 'd, 'm*, plus *'s* for closed elision hosts only ([measurement:contractions]): 300 instances, 17.09 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. Against them, counting whole phrases *do not, does not, did not, is not, are not, was not, were not, cannot, could not, would not, should not, will not, have not, has not, had not* ([measurement:uncontracted-negatives]): only 9 uncontracted negative phrases in the entire corpus, 0.51 per 1,000 words, 5/10 samples. Write *don't*, not *do not*. The uncontracted form is so rare that reaching for it marks the sentence as anomalous.

**Profanity is present and purposeful.** Counting per the prose-author corpus-rates profanity rule ([measurement:profanity-vulgarity]): 26 instances, 1.48 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, once or twice per piece. It lands at moments of maximum absurdity or contempt — *"tell the cartel to fuck off"* (`2026-07-09-wilhoitian.txt`), *"the whole fucking point"* (`2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt`) — not scattered as general register. Reach for it at the single moment of highest outrage in the piece.

**Rhetorical questions throughout.** Counting every literal question mark ([measurement:question-marks]): 38 instances, 2.17 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, several times per piece. The questions are almost never genuine requests; they reformulate the argument as an invitation. *"If you've got a chatbot that can teach my kids, why sell it to my local school district? Why not just open a school?"* (`2026-07-13-go-meta-meta.txt`).

**Parenthetical asides are frequent.** Counting non-nested round-bracket pairs on a single line ([measurement:round-parenthetical-spans]): 97 pairs, 5.53 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples, throughout. They carry jokes, qualifications, and snark: *(very, very weird)*; *(but I repeat myself)*; *(a direct quote)*. URLs are posted bare on their own lines, not inside parentheses.

**Main claims are stated flat; first-person markers flag speculation.** *"This is bullshit"* (`2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`); *"Meritocracy cashes out to a eugenic belief in royal blood"* (`2026-07-16-lucky-orifices.txt`). When a claim is speculative rather than argumentative, *"I think"* flags it: *"I think billionaire solipsism can account for much of the malinvestment in this obvious bubble, but I don't think it's the whole story"* (`2026-07-24-supplemental-income.txt`) — 7/10 samples. The move "I think X, but I think there's also Y" introduces a secondary argument, not a softened primary one.

**Named opponents and allies.** Argument runs against named institutions and individuals (Uber, Musk, Thiel, Trump, Zuckerberg, Apple) and builds on named allies and sources (Lina Khan, David Weil, John Quiggin, Tim O'Reilly, Corey Robin) — 10/10 samples, throughout. Allies are attributed in appositives: *"As Lina Khan likes to say..."*, *"As Weil writes..."* Neither target nor source is left anonymous when a name is available.

**Interruption punctuation: en-dash only.** Counting every literal en-dash character ([measurement:en-dashes]): 73 instances, 4.16 per 1,000 words, 10/10 samples. Against that, counting every literal em-dash character ([measurement:em-dashes]): 0 instances, 0/10 samples establish the absence. Use en-dash (–) as the sentence-level interrupter. Never em-dash (—).

## 5. Figures

Analogies reach into three domains: **everyday commercial transactions** (the escrow agent and the deed, the restaurateur scheduling servers, the baker avoiding sawdust); **bodily experience** (bladders, kidneys, orifices, piss); **games, races, and gambling** (the beauty contest, outrunning the bear market, picks and shovels in a gold rush) — 9/10 samples. Each analogy is one or two sentences long and is not returned to; a figure makes contact and is never reopened.

The author also borrows terms coined by others and uses them as analytical levers: "dickover" (Gruber), "AI Omelas" (Le Guin), "go meta" (Rushkoff), "the mirror world" (Klein) — 7/10 samples. The borrowed term is named with attribution and then extended without apology.

I cannot bound "a figure" for counting purposes. The countable part is the vocabulary these figures draw from — the three domain lists above. Use vocabulary from those domains; reach outside them only when the analogy is genuinely stronger.

## 6. Register range

The register is polemical throughout. Two excursions appear: in `2026-07-21-dickovers.txt`, the register becomes instructional — named keyboard shortcuts, specific extension names, step-by-step procedures — with argument subordinated to the how-to. In `2026-07-14-designated-survivor.txt` (and partially in others), the register shifts into the biographical — cancer treatment, a dead friend, literary executor arrangements offered as evidence — 4/10 samples. In both excursions, the short verdict sentence, the contractions, and the inclusive "we" persist. The style fingerprint does not change when the register shifts.

## 7. What the corpus never does

Structure is carried inside the prose. Topic shifts are marked by a new paragraph that opens on the new subject's name or a short transitional sentence — 10/10 samples (`2026-07-13-go-meta-meta.txt`: the move from the Khayyam epigraph into gig economics is a paragraph break followed by "This is a question that needs to be forcefully put to AI hucksters"). Nothing in the corpus uses a subheading, a bulleted list, or a numbered section to organize argument. When `2026-07-23-drop-a-dime.txt` reaches for a list — *"Step one: Exist. Step two: There is no step two"* — it uses the list form to mock the absence of steps, not to enumerate them.

Em-dash (—) does not appear: [measurement:em-dashes] 0 instances, all 10 samples establish the absence. En-dash (–) does the same structural work at 4.16 per 1,000 words. Use en-dash; never em-dash.

## 8. What this profile could not determine

voice.md is empty; all observations are derived from corpus alone.

All ten samples come from a two-week run of blog posts in a single polemical register. Nothing here shows how this voice operates in fiction, private correspondence, or any genre where sustained argument is not the purpose.

Dropped observations: 4 — the "named syllogism / QED" rhetorical move (concentrated in `2026-07-16-lucky-orifices.txt`, insufficient cross-sample support for a general habit); URL-as-citation structure (a format habit, not a prose one); coined neologisms for new phenomena (present across the corpus but no enumerable component could be defined without judgment calls about what constitutes a coinage vs. a borrowed term); the use of direct imperatives to the reader as a class (present in the instructional piece but too register-specific to generalise).
